title: The Cachy-Dehn Theorem
text:
The Cauchy-Dehn Theorem

Theorem. (Cauchy-Dehn)   Let \(P\) be polytope of dimension \(d\ge 3\). If \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}:V\to\Bbb R^d\) restricts to a trivial first-order motion on every facet of \(P\), then \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}\) is itself trivial.

We prove something slightly different that is phrased entirely in terms of frameworks and first-order rigidity. For this let the braced skeleton of a polytope \(P\) be its skeleton with additional bars between vertices that share an incident facet (i.e. each facet of \(P\) turns into a complete graph on its vertices). The proof of Cauchy-Dehn from this is equivalent to the proof of the Corollary stated above.

Theorem.  The braced skeleton of a \(d\)-polytope, \(d\ge 2\), is first-order rigid.

For those who know how an analogue of Cauchy’s theorem is usually proven in hgher dimension knows that one usually needs to alternatve between Euclidan and spherical polytopes. This can be avoided for infinitesimal rigidity (if you will, a consequence of the fact that spherical and Euclidean first-order theory are equivalent).
Proof.
The proof is by induction on the dimension \(d\ge 3\) of the polytope.
The statement is clear for \(d=2\), and \(d=3\) is precisely the Corollary from the introduction.
For the induction step we assume \(d>3\). Note first that \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}\) stays an infinitseimal motion of \(G\) if we add further bars between any two vertices that are in the same facet (i.e. each face becomes a complete graph). We shall call the result a braced skeleton of \(P\).
Fix a vertex \(v\) of \(P\). Choose a hyplerplane \(H\) that separates it from the other vertices of \(P\). The intersection \(Q:=P\cap H\) is a vertex figure of \(P\) at \(v\) (this is the step where in Cauchy’s theorem we need to use a sphere instead of a hyperplane and hence need to work with spherical polytopes). Consider the braced skeleton of \(Q\) as a framework in \(H\). It is infinitesmally rigid by induction hypothesis. It is easy to see (1-extensions) that coning over \(v\) preserves nfnitseimal rgidty.
Observe now that the sub-framework of \(G\) on \(v\) and its neighbors can be obtained by radial moves from \(v\). Since radial moves preserve infinitesimal rigidity (see this earlier blog post) wefind that this “vertex framework” is infinitiseimally rigid aswell.
For the last step recall that a trivial infinitsimal motion is determined by its value on \(d\) affinely independen points. We have seen that on each facet and on each vertex neighborhood \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}\) is trivial. But if the vertex \(v\) lies in the facet \(F\), then the corresponding frameworks overlap in a complete affinely spanning framework on \(d\)-vertices,hence give rise to the same trivial motion. Since the vertex-facet incidewnce fraph of a polytope is connected, weobtain the concluion.
\(\square\)
The following is a simple consequence.

Corollary.  If \(P\) is a polytope of dimension \(d\ge 3\) and \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}:V\to\Bbb R^d\) restricts to a trivial first-order motion on each 2-face, then \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}\) is itself a trivial first-order motion.

title: The Cachy-Dehn Theorem
text:
Some background
One of the big classical theorems in the rigidty of polyhedra is the following:

Theorem. (Dehn)  The skeleton of a convex simplicial polyhedron is infinitesimally rigid.

Here and in the following “polyhedon” means a 3-dmensional polytope, and the skeleton of a polytope is the framework that consists of the polytopes vertices and edges. The proof of Dehn’s theorem shares many elements with the proof of Cauchy’s famous rigidity theorem, though turns out less technical in the details.
One reason that Cauchy’s theorem is formulates for simplicial polyhedra is that simplicial polyhedra can be treated as bar-joint frameworks, and so their rigidity theory, and in particular the notion of infinitesimal rigidity, is well-known. If one aims to prove, or even express, a similar statement for non-simplicial polyhedra, one needs to say more about the notion of infinitesimal rigidity. This is of course possibe (e.g. formalized by point-hyperplane frameworks), but this can also be entirely avoided as shown by the following strengthenings of Dehn’s theorem:

Whiteley: still true for non-simpliciation polyhedra if we triangulate the faces without introducing new vertices.
Alexandrov: still true if we introduce new vertices along the natural edges and then triangulate.
Connelly: if we introduce new vertices in the interior of faces (and then triangulate), then the skeleton is no longer infinitesimally rigid, but still prestress stable (and therefore second-order rigid).

There is a way to formulate Dehn’s theorem for genera polyhedra while also avoiding the language of point-hyperplane frameworks:

Corollary 1.  Let \(P\subset\Bbb R^3\) be a convex polyhedron. If \(\boldsymbol v:V(P)\to\Bbb R^3\) restrict to a trivial first-order motion on each facet \(F\subset P\), then \(\boldsymbol v\) is itself a trivial first-order motion. 

In this form it is clear how to formulate a generalization to higher dimensions. This generalization is also known as the Cauchy-Dehn theorem:

Theorem. (Cauchy-Dehn)  Let \(P\subset\Bbb R^d\) be a convex polyhedron of dimension \(d\ge 3\). If \(\boldsymbol v:V(P)\to\Bbb R^d\) restrict to a trivial first-order motion on each facet \(F\subset P\), then \(\boldsymbol v\) is itself a trivial first-order motion.

text:
Spherical frameworks and poltopes
A spherical framework is a frameworks \((G,\boldsymbol p)\) whose vertices are confined to a sphere, that is, \(\boldsymbol p\subset\Bbb S^d\). The rigidity theory of spherical frameworks considered only motions that keep all vertices on the sphere. A simple consequence of this is that infinitesimal motions happen tangent to the sphere, or more precisely, \(\langle p_i,\dot p_i\rangle=0\) for all \(i\in V\).
Of course, spherical frameworks can be studied with the usual rigidity theory of frameworks by considering them as coned frameworks with a cone vertex fixed at the center of the sphere.

title: The Cauchy-Dehn Theorem
text:
Proving the Cauchy-Dehn Theorem

Theorem. (Cauchy-Dehn)  Let \(P\subset\Bbb R^d\) be a convex polyhedron of dimension \(d\ge 3\). If \(\boldsymbol v:V(P)\to\Bbb R^d\) restrict to a trivial first-order motion on each facet \(F\subset P\), then \(\boldsymbol v\) is itself a trivial first-order motion.

To prove this theorem we first turn it into a statement about frameworks. More precisely, we simulate rigid facets by turning each facet into a rigid framework.
For this let the braced skeleton of a polytope \(P\) be its skeleton with additional bars between vertices that share an incident facet (i.e. each facet of \(P\) turns into a complete graph on its vertices). We will later see that the braced skeleton of a polytope is first-order rigid (and in fact, much less additional bars are needed). However, for the initial proof we need to add even more structure. The reenforced skeleton of a polytope is obtained from its braced skeleton by adding new vertices, one new vertex \(v_F\) per facet \(F\), placing it somewhere outside of \(\operatorname{aff}(F)\), and adding bars between \(v_F\) and all vertices of \(F\). In the reinforced skeleton the vertices of \(F\) and \(v_F\) together form a complete framework.

We prove something slightly different that is phrased entirely in terms of frameworks and first-order rigidity. For this let the braced skeleton of a polytope \(P\) be its skeleton with additional bars between vertices that share an incident facet (i.e. each facet of \(P\) turns into a complete graph on its vertices). The proof of Cauchy-Dehn from this is equivalent to the proof of the Corollary stated above.
For those who know how an analogue of Cauchy’s theorem is usually proven in hgher dimension knows that one usually needs to alternatve between Euclidan and spherical polytopes. This can be avoided for infinitesimal rigidity (if you will, a consequence of the fact that spherical and Euclidean first-order theory are equivalent).

Theorem.  A reenforced skeleton of a \(d\)-polytope, \(d\ge 3\), is first-order rigid.

Proof.
We use induction on the dimension \(d\ge 3\) of the polytope. The induction base \(d=3\) was proven in Corollary 1. We therefore assume \(d>3\).
For each vertex \(i\) of \(P\) we choose a hyperplane \(H_i\) that separates \(p_i\) from all other vertices. The intersection \(Q_i:=P\cap H_i\) is a \((d-1)\)-dimensional polytope (known as the vertex figure of \(P\) at \(i\)) to which we later apply the induction hypothesis.
Let \((G_i,\boldsymbol p)\) be the sub-framework of the reenforced skeleton induced on vertex \(i\) and all its neighbors. Observe that this is a coned framework with apex \(p_i\), and each edge from \(p_i\) intersects \(H_i\). Through radial moves we can move each neighbor of \(p_i\) to lie on \(H_i\). Let’s call this new framework \((G_i',\boldsymbol q_i)\), and let \((G_i'',\boldsymbol q_i)\) be its sub-framework without the apex \(i\).
If we consider \((G_i'',\boldsymbol q_i)\) as a \((d-1)\)-dimensional framework in \(H_i\) then it is a reenforced skeleton of \(Q_i\). This follows from the fact that each facet \(F'\) of \(Q_i\) is of the form \(F'=F\cap H_i\) for some facet \(F\) of \(P\), and that the neighbors of \(i\) in \(F\) also form a complete graph. The radially moved counterpart of the reenforcement vertex \(p_F\) becomes the reenforcement vertex for \(F'\).
By induction hypothesis we can now conclude that \((G_i'',\boldsymbol q_i)\) is first-order rigid. It is well-known that coning preserves first-order rigidity (a short reminder is given in the end of this article). That is, \((G_i',\boldsymbol q_i)\) is first-order rigid as well. Finally, since radial moves in a coned framework preserve first-order rigidity (see this earlier blog post), we can conclude that also \((G_i,\boldsymbol p)\) is first-order rigid.
We have now established that \(\boldsymbol v\) restrict to a trivial motion on each \((G_i,\boldsymbol p)\) and \((G_F,\boldsymbol p)\). It remains to show that it is the same trivial motion on all of them. For this, observe that if vertex \(i\) and facet \(F\) are incident, then the frameworks \((G_i,\boldsymbol p)\) and \((G_F,\boldsymbol p)\) intersect in an affinely spanning sub-framework. Since a trivial motion is completely determined by its value on a set of affinely spanning points, we can conclude that the trivial motion is indeed the same on \((G_i,\boldsymbol p)\) and \((G_F,\boldsymbol p)\). Since the vertex-facet incidence graph of a polytope is connected, the conclusion follows.

\(\square\)



Similar to Cauchy’s rigidity theorem it appears natural to now prove a version of Cauchy-Dehn that only imposes rigidity constraints on the 2-faces. To my surprise, I was not able to prove this. Hence I formulate it here as a conjecture:

Conjecture.  Let \(P\subset\Bbb R^d\) be a polytope of dimension \(d\ge 3\):

The framework obtained from the skeleton of \(P\) by adding edges so that all 2-faces are triangulates, is infinitesimally rigid.
If a map \(\boldsymbol v:V\to \Bbb R^d\) restricts to a trivial motion on each 2-face of \(P\), then \(\boldsymbol v\) is a trivial motion itself.





Lemma. (Coning preserves rigidity)   Let \((G^*, \boldsymbol p)\) a \((d+1)\)-dimensional framework that is a cone over its \(d\)-dimensional sub-frameworks \((G,\boldsymbol p)\). Then \((G^*, \boldsymbol p)\) is first-order rigid if and only if \((G, \boldsymbol p)\) is first-order rigid. 

Proof.
Let \(R\) and \(R^*\) be the rigidity matrices of the frameworks. Observe that
\[\begin{align}
\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}R^*
&= \mathop{\mathrm{corank}}(R^*)^\top + (d+1)(V+1) - (E+V)
\\
&= (\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}R^\top + dV-E) + d + V + 1 - V
\\
&= \mathop{\mathrm{corank}}R + d + 1.
\end{align}\]
It follows that \(\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}R={d+1\choose 2}\) if and only if \(\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}R^*={d+2\choose 2}\). \(\square\)

title: The Cachy-Dehn Theorem
text:
Spherical frameworks and spherical polytopes
A spherical framework of dimension \(d\) is a frameworks \((G,\boldsymbol p)\) with vertices confined to a \(d\)-dimensional sphere, say for simplicity, the standard unit sphere \(\Bbb S^d\subset\Bbb R^{d+1}\). Naturally, the rigidity theory of spherical frameworks considers only motions that keep all vertices on this sphere. Luckily, rigidity theory needs not be reinvented for this setting because spherical frameworks can be modelled by (Euclidean) coned framework where the cone vertex is fixed to the center of the sphere. With this, all aspects of the well-known Euclidean rigidity theory transfer straight-forwardly to the spherical setting.
First-order motions point tangent to the sphere, or more precisely, \(\langle p_i,\dot p_i\rangle=0\) for all \(i\in V\). A trivial first-order motion is of the form \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}=S\boldsymbol p\) where \(S\) is a skew symmetric matrix (no infinitesimal translation is necessary).
A spherical polytope in turn is the intersection of a polyhedral cone \(C\) with the unit sphere \(\Bbb S^d\). Its faces correspond to the faces of the polyhedral cone.

Theorem. (Cauchy-Dehn for spherical polytopes)   Let \(P\) be a spherical polytope of dimension \(d\ge 3\). If \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}:V\to\Bbb R^{d+1}\) restricts to a trivial first-order motion on every facet of \(P\), then \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}\) is trivial. 

We prove this statement here assuming that the respective statement is already known for Euclidean polytopes.
Proof. We can write \(P=C\cap\Bbb S^d\) for a polyheral cone \(C\). Let \(H\) be a hyperplane tangent to \(\Bbb S^d\) in some interior point of \(P\). Then \(P':=C\cap H\) is a (Euclidean) polytope. Let \(F'\subset P'\) be a facet and \(F\subset P\) the corresponding facet in \(P\). By assumption \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}\) restricts to a trivial motion on \(F\), that is, \(\dot p_i = Sp_i\) for some skew-symmetric matrix \(S\). We claim that the restriction of \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}\) to \(F'\) is a trivial first-order motion in \(H\simeq\Bbb R^d\).
\(\square\)

Theorem. (Cauchy-Dehn for spherical polytopes)   Let \(P\) be a spherical polytope of dimension \(d\ge 3\). If \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}:V\to\Bbb R^{d+1}\) restricts to a trivial first-order motion on every facet of \(P\), then \(\dot{\boldsymbol p}\) is trivial.

title: The non-symmetric Mahler conjecture and self-polar polytopes
text:
The Mahler conjecture is usually stated for centrally symmetric convex bodies. However, its non-symmetric version seems equally interesting and intractable. As it turns out, the non-symmetric version has a neat formulation in terms of the volume (not Mahler volume) of self-polar bodies. \(\DeclareMathOperator{\vol}{vol}\)

Given a centrally symmetric convex body \(B\subset\Bbb R^d\), Kurt Mahler defined the following linearly invariant “notion of volume”, now known as the Mahler volume:
\[
M(B):=\operatorname{vol}(B)\cdot\operatorname{vol}(B^\circ).
\]
Here \(B^\circ:=\{y\in\Bbb R^d\mid \langle x,y\rangle\le 1\text{ for all }x\in B\}\) denotes the polar dual of \(B\). It has long been known that the Mahler volume is maximized for the sphere (this is known as the Blaschke-Santaló inequality). In contrast, the minimizers seem elusive. It has equally long been conjectured that the cube has the minimal Mahler volume: for every centrally symmetric convex body \(B\subset\Bbb R^d\) holds
\[M(B)\ge M(\text{$d$-cube}) = \frac{4^d}{d!}.\]
This is known as the Mahler conjecture, which, as of today, remains open. In his blog post Terrence Tao makes a suggestion for why the conjecture might be so hard:

In my opinion, the main reason why this conjecture is so difficult is that unlike the upper bound, in which there is essentially only one extremiser up to affine transformations (namely the ball), there are many distinct extremisers for the lower bound – not only the cube and the octahedron, but also products of cubes and octahedra, polar bodies of products of cubes and octahedra, products of polar bodies of … well, you get the idea. It is really difficult to conceive of any sort of flow or optimisation procedure which would converge to exactly these bodies and no others […]

(this family of conjectured extremizers he refers to is known as the Hanner polytopes)
There is however an easy way to see that the multitude of minimizers cannot be the true or only reason here: by dropping the assumption of central symmetry we obtain the non-symmetric Mahler conjecture. It asserts that the simplex minimizes the Mahler volume among all convex bodies:
\[M(B)\ge M(\text{$d$-simplex}) = \frac{(d+1)^{d+1}}{(d!)^2}.\]
This conjecture has turned out equally intractable. Yet, since we expect the simplex to be the unique minimizer, Terry’s explanation cannot apply.
We briefly addres an important technicality with the non-symmetric version: computing the Mahler volume requires computing the polar body, which is not a translation invariant construction. If \(B\) is centrally symmetric, there is a preferred choice of origin (the symmetry center). For a general body there is no such preferred choice and computing the Mahler volume requires fixing the bodies location relative to the origin. However, there exists a unique point \(x\in P\) (the Sataló point) that, if chosen as the origin, minimizes the Mahler volume.

Volume products vs. volume sums
Another point that the hardness of the Mahler conjecture os often attributed to is the fact that is deals with volume products. In some sense, one might say, volumes are node made to be multiplied.
Here is a simple counterargument to show that the products is also not the source of the hardness.

Lemma.  The (symmetric) Mahler conjecture is equivalent to the statement \[\vol(K)+\vol(K^\circ) \ge \frac{2^{d+1}}{\sqrt{d!}}\]

Since the Mahler volume is affine invariant, we can rescale \(K\) until \(\vol(K)=\vol(K^\circ)\), and hence \(M(K)=\vol(K)^2\). If the Mahler conjecture holds, we obtain
\[\vol(K)+\vol(K^\circ)=2\vol(K)=2\sqrt{M(K)} \ge \frac{2^{d+1}}{\sqrt{d!}}.\]
Suppose now that our alterantive conjecture holds. For a convex body \(K\) let \(\tilde K=\lambda K\) be so that \(\vol(\tilde K)=\vol(\tilde K^\circ)\). 
\[\vol(K)+\vol(K^\circ) = \vol(\tilde K/\lambda) + \vol((\tilde K/\lambda)^\circ) = \Big(\frac1{\lambda^d}+\lambda^d\Big)\vol(\tilde K) \ge 2\vol(\tilde K).\]
We can assume that we have chosen \(\lambda\) so as to miimize the left-hand side. That is, we chose \(\lambda=1\), or \(\K=\tilde K\). Since our volume sum conjecture is assumed ton hold for \(\tilde K\), we obtain
\[M(K)=M(\tilde K)=\vol(\tilde K)^2 \ge \Big(\frac12 \frac{2^{d+1}}{\sqrt{d!}}\Big)^2=\frac{4^d}{d!}.\]
Yes, sure, the volume sum is not affine invariant and therefore more cumbersome to work with for other reasons. But the point stays, that the complexity did not intriinsically stem from the volume product.
The argument above is of course entirely independent of the symmetry of the polytope and we can formulate the volume sum conjecture also in the unsymmetric case:
\[\vol(K)+\vol(K^\circ)\ge \frac{(d+1)^{\frac{d+1}2}}{d!}.\]
This sum formulation does indeed help since it leads to a decoupling. The volume can be written down as a sum of volumes of orthoschemes. This decomposition is preserved under polar duality. Hence, the volume sum can be written down as a sum of volume sums over the flags of the polytope.


Volumes of self-polar bodies
The goal here is to reformulate the non-symmetric Mahler conjecture in terms of volumes of self-polar bodies, thereby avoiding volume products entirely.

A convex body \(B\) is self-polar if \(B\) and \(B^\circ\) are isometric (or equivalently, related by an orthogonal transformation). An example is the unit ball; not however a ball of any other radius: if \(B\) is a ball of radius \(r\) then \(B^\circ\) has radius \(1/r\), which is non-isometric to \(B\). We see that self-polarity cares about scale. Another example is a simplex, if chosen of a suitable shape and scale. In this case \(B=-B^\circ\).
The following conjecture is equivalent to the non-symmetric Mahler conjecture:

Conjecture.  The simplex has the smallest volume among all self-polar bodies.

One direction of the equivalence is straight-forward: if \(B\) is self-polar, then
\[\llap{(*)\qquad}M(B)=\vol(B)\cdot\vol(B^\circ)=\vol(B)^2.\]
Hence, if simplices minimizes \(M(\,\cdot\,)\), then since they are also self-polar, \((*)\) simplices also minimize \(\vol(\,\cdot\,)\) among all self-polar bodies.
For the other direction we need to recall the join operation \(B_1\star B_2\), and the following properties:

if \(B_1,B_2\) are of dimension \(d_1,d_2\) respectively, then \(B_1\star B_2\) is of dimension \(d_1+d_2+1\).
we can explicitle compute the volume of joins: \[\vol(B_1\star B_2) = c(d_1,d_2)\cdot \vol(B_1)\cdot\vol(B_2),\]where \(c(d_1,d_2)\) depends on the dimensions of the bodies, but not on the bodies themselves.
joins commute with the polar dual operation: \((B_1\star B_2)^\circ = B_1^\circ\star B_2^\circ\). In particular, \(B\star B^\circ\) is always a self-polar body!
joins of simplices yield simplices: \(\Delta_{d_1}\star\Delta_{d_2} = \Delta_{d_1+d_2+1}\). Moreover, if we start from simplices in their self-polar realization of minimal volume, the join is also a self-polar simplex in self-polar realization of minimal volume.

Formulating these properties precisely requires some more care and a carefully chosen geometric realization of the join. See my previous blog entry on the join for the details.
Suppose then that \(P\) is a counterexample to the non-symmetric Mahler conjecture, that is, \(M(P)<M(\Delta_d)\). Then \(P\star P^\circ\) is a self-polar polytope with
\[
\begin{align}
\vol(P\star P^\circ) &= c\cdot \vol(P)\cdot \vol(P^\circ)
\\ &= c\cdot M(P)
\\ &< c \cdot M(\Delta_d)
\\ &= c \cdot \vol(\Delta_d)\cdot\vol(\Delta_d^\circ)
\\ &= c \cdot \vol(\Delta_d)\cdot\vol(\Delta_d)
\\ &= \vol(\Delta_d\star\Delta_d)
= \vol(\Delta_{2d+1}).
\end{align}
\]
that is, a counterexample to Conjecture A. Conversely, Conjecture A implies the non-symmetric Mahler conjecture.
Conversely, suppose that \(P\) is a self-polar polytope with \(\vol(P)<\vol(\Delta_d)\). Then
\[M(B)=\vol(B)\cdot\vol(B^\circ)=\vol(B)^2 \ge \vol(\Delta_d)^2=\vol(\Delta_d)\cdot\vol(\Delta_d^\circ) = M(\Delta_d),\]
which is a counterexample to the non-symmetric Mahler conjecture.
Self-polar polytopes are not very well understood. For example, it is unknown whether every self-dual polytope has a self-polar realization.
Finally, I am not aware of an analogous formulation for the symmetric Mahler conjecture. Of course, one could ask for the smallest volume of a convex body of the form \(B*B^\circ\), whether \(B\) is centrally symmetric. This however feels not like a significant reformulation and does not have the charme of a natural problem on its own.
I do yet believe that this reformulation of the non-symmetric Mahler conjecture makes any signifiante progress towards its resolution. If anything, it likely shows that self-polar bodies are very complicated objects.

What about the symmetric Mahler conjecture?
Admittedly, there exists a quite analogous formulation for the symmetric Mahler conjecture. The main difference is that
…
Clearly \(\vol(B\times B^\circ)=\vol(B)\vol(B^\circ)\). Not as obvious, but not super hard either, we have
\[\vol(B*B^\circ)=\frac{d}{d+1}\cdot\vol(B)\vol(B^\circ).\]
Thus, we could ask: what is the smallest volume of a body of the form \(B\times B^\circ\)?
In the end, the attractiveness of the reformulation in the non-symmetric case comes mainly from the fact that bodies of the form \(B\star B^\circ\) are contained in the elegantly describable class of self-polar bodies. We could as well ahve asked for the smallest volume of a body of the form \(B\star B^\circ\) or of an even-dimensional self-polar body with polarity map
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
-1 & &
\\
& & I
\\
& I &
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

title: Three conjectures on polytope reconstruction
text:
Polytope reconstruction asks in how far a convex polytope is determined by partial combinatorial and geometric data. For example, if I give you just the graph of the polytope, can you reconstruct its dimension and the rest of the combinatorial type? If I give you the combinatorial type together with some edge lengths, does this determine the shape of the polytope?
In this post I present three of my favorite conjectures in this regime. All three conjectures have in common that they assume knowledge of the graph of the polytope and its edge lengths.

Polyhedra and angular defects
The rigidity theory of polyhedra (i.e. 3-dimensional polytopes) is a classical topic. Famously, Cauchy’s rigidity theorem asserts that a polyhedron is determined by its edge lengths and face angles. That edge lengths alone can fail to determine the shape of a polyhedron is topic of a recent article of mine with Matthias Himmelmann and Bernd Schulze. It remains open what minimal additional data suffices. The following seems to be among the most elementary open question in this regard:

Conjecture I   A polyhedron is determined by its graph, edge length and angular defects. 

At each vertex \(v\) of the polytope, the angular defect measures how much is missing from \(v\) becoming flat, that is, \(\tau_v:=2\pi-\sum_{\sigma} \alpha_{v\sigma}\), where the sum is over all faces \(\sigma\) incident to \(v\), and \(\alpha_{v\sigma}\) is the interior angle of \(\sigma\) at \(v\). I asked this question on MathOverflow and the responses make me think that I stumbled upon something non-trivial.
An early thought I had was to use the lengths and angular defects to reconstruct the metric of the polyhedron’s surface and then use Alexandrov’s uniqueness theorem. But I don’t know whether this is possible.


Pointed polytopes
Let’s move on to polytopes of general dimensions. The new difficulty here is that the edge graph does no longer determine the rest of the combinatorics or even the dimension of the polytope.
A pointed polytope consists of a polytope \(P\subset\Bbb R^d\) and a point \(x\in\operatorname{int}(P)\). The distance of the vertices of \(P\) to the point \(x\) we call the radii of \(P\).

Conjecture II   A pointed polytope is determined by its graph, edge lengths and radii. 

This is the central Conjecture 1.1 from my article “Rigidity, Tensegrity and Reconstruction of Polytopes under Metric Constraints”. There I use Wachspress Geometry to confirm it in three special cases:

if the polytope is centrally symmetric,
if we prescribe the combinatorial type,
if we look only in a small neighborhood of a given polytope.

I strongly believe that Conjecture II is true in general. A promising approach is provided in Lemma 4.3 of the same paper.
I also just recently realized that this conjecture is equivalent to an older conjecture of mine from “Capturing Polytopal Symmetries by Coloring the Edge-Graph”.

Conjecture II’   All combinatorial symmetries of the edge graph of a pointed polytope that preserve edge lengths and radii extend to isometries of the polytope itself. 

The idea behind the equivalence is the following: if there are two pointed polytopes \(P\) and \(Q\) with the same graph, edge lengths and radii, then \(P\times P\), \(P\times Q\) and \(Q\times Q\) are also three polytopes with the same graph, lengths and radii. The polytopes are however of the same dimension but with different symmetries. In particular, it follows that for Conjecture II we may assume that we know the dimension.


Combinatorial types from edge lengths
Let’s return to un-pointed polytopes. I feel least certain about the following conjecture, but counterexamples seem out of reach as well:

Conjecture III   The combinatorial type of a polytope is determined by its graph and edge lengths. 

I think that, if true, this conjecture will be hard to prove because of the strong consequences it has. For example, it would resolve Conjecture II because it reduces it to the solved special case where the combinatorics is known. Another fun implication is a strengthening of Cauchy’s rigidity theorem in higher dimensions. Usually, Cauchy’s theorem is stated there as follows: if we prescribe the combinatorial type and the shapes of all 2-faces, then the shape of the polytope is fixed. A consequence of Conjecture III is that it suffices to provide only the absolutely necessary combinatorics: instead of the full face lattice, we only provide the edge graph and 2-faces, but nothing above. From the 2-face shapes we can obtain the edge lengths, then the full combinatorics via Conjecture III, and hence the full shape by Chauchy’s classical theorem.

title: Writing Guide
text:
Over the years I gathered some habits in writing math in TeX. Some of which I considered good style, other I consider as minimal requirements for publishing. Many I see violated regularly in all kinds of publications.
But the best tools can be used to create bad looking articles.

Consistency
The most important rule in all of technical writing is to be consistent! It encompasses many of the points I mention below. Consistency means that you might make arbitrary choices, but you need to make the same arbitrary choice throughout your document. This applies to writing style, variable naming and meaning, styles of figures, color themes, margins and spacing, word choice and phrasing, labelling, numbering, emphasize, how you address the reader, and who you are writing for.

be consistent in the adderssed audience, with a slight caveat: the level of sophistication of the aimed at audience might monotonically incrase throughout the writing. There is no need to define determinant if your article is about higher category theory.
be consistent in naming: don’t use \(\Delta\)-Y-transformations sometimes, and \(\Delta Y\)-transformations other times. Stick to one.
be consistent in formatting. I like to write “i.e.” in italic. If you do so as well, don’t also write “i.e.” at other places.



General tips

If you don’t know the right TeX command for a math symbol, you can use Detexify.
If some notations are too cumbersome for you to type over and over, you can always introduce a command. Some examples where I do this are given below.
If you are not sure about the style you want (should the sphere be denoted as \(\Bbb S^2\) or \(\mathbf S^2\)?), introduce a command for it (e.g. \sphere) so you can later change it globally if necessary.
Curious about any TeX code below? Right click on th math and select Show Math As > TeX Commands.



Non-negotiable
The following style related bullet point are very important to me and are, if not followed, a sign of general carelessness regarding the reading experience.

Pay attention to always use math mode when you type math, especially for single letter variables: v is not a variable, but \(v\) is.
Font matters: \(S\), \(\mathrm S\), \(\mathbf S\) and \(\mathcal S\) are all different symbols and denote different variables. They are not interchangeable.
\(cos\) is not the cosine function. It is the product of three variables \(c\), \(o\) and \(s\). For the cosine use \cos which renders as \(\cos\). If the function you need is not available as a command, make your own using \DeclareMathOperator. Likewise, \(dx\) is not a differential. Use, for example, \mathrm dx to typeset \(\mathrm dx\). Consider intrudcing the command \dx if you need this often.
Write \(i\in\{1,...,n\}\) instead of \(i=1,...,n\). Also better avoid \(1\le i \le n\) because it will make problems in certain cases such as in “for all \(a\le i\le b\)” where it might seem you write “for all \(a\) …”.
Use approrpiate paranthesis sizing \[
{\color{red}\mathrm x}\;\;({n\choose k}+n)
\quad\text{vs}\quad
{\color{ForestGreen}\checkmark}\,\;\Big({n\choose k}+n\Big)
\quad\text{vs}\quad
{\color{ForestGreen}\checkmark}\,\;\left(\!{n\choose k}+n\right).
\] You can adjust the paranthesis size automatically using the \left and \right commands, or manually using \big, \Big and \Bigg. I actually prefer the middle over the right one, but this is a matter of taste.
Use the correct vertial line symbol. There is a difference in how spacing works for the pipes character \(|\) versus the command \mid, which also renders as \(\mid\). For example, in set builder notation \[
\{n\in \Bbb N| n^2=9\}
\quad\text{vs}\quad
\{n\in \Bbb N \mid n^2=9\}
\] only \mid gives the corres spacing. Unfortunately, \mid cannot be grown using \Big or \middle commands, so one needs to use pipes there. One must then ensure correct spacing manually, for example, using \, and \;. \[
\Big\{n\in \Bbb N \;\Big |\; {n \choose 2}=9\Big\}
\quad\text{vs}\quad
\Big\{n\in \Bbb N \mid {n \choose 2} n^2=9\Big\}
\]
Don’t use similarly looking symbols to get the job done. TeX puts a lot of effort in the correct spacing. Research whether there is a correct symbol. It has never been taht simple, using ChatGPT or Detexify. Here are some examples of misuse.
Never write \(<a,b>\), always write \(\langle a,b \rangle\) using \langle and \rangle. I use custom commands \< and \>.
Correctly use binary operators and their big versions: \[
A\bigcap B
\quad\text{vs}\quad
A\cap B
\qquad\quad
\cap_{i\in I} S_i,
\quad\text{vs}\quad
\bigcap_{i\in I} S_i
.\]
Don’t use too large inline formulas because it will make the line spacing inconsistent. Here is an outrageou example: \(\sum_{\substack{k=0\\k\equiv 0\pmod 2}}^{n^2} k^2\). To fix this, either use less spatious notation where possible, or use a display formulas instead.
Don’t write \(a_1+...+a_n\) but \(a_1+\cdots+a_n\) using the \cdots command (you can tell that using ... the spacing is off). I admit I rarely use \ldots, I prefer the good old .... One could introduce a command \... to be flexible on this.
Use correct spacing after non-period punctuation: if you write Prof. Dr. Miller, this will render incorrectly since TeX reads . as the end of a sentence and therefore introduces too much stretchable space after the period. You need to write Prof.\ Dr.\ Miller.
To describe a map that send, e.g., \(x\) to its square, write \(x\mapsto x^2\) using \mapsto, not \(x\to x^2\).



Good notation

avoid too many nested sub- and superscripts: \(H^{n_2}_{m_n^2}\). Preferably don’t go beydont the second layer, use thrid layer sparingly.



For the extra oomph

As a general rule of thumb, numbers up to twelve are spelled out in letters, while numbers beyond this are written with digits. For example, “this proof only works in dimension three”, whereas “the Leech lattice lives in dimension 24”. There are exceptions to these rules and the exact handling is a matter of taste. Here are some unacceptable uses: “there are 3 different cases we need to consider”. However, if the number could have been a non-integer, I always use digits: “evaluating this integral yield 2”.
Emphasize your definitions. Either through font or color or, ideally, both. This way it is easier for the reader to locate the definition of a term or symbol when needed. Avoid using bold face for definitions, which is reserved for headings. I like to use color because one should not use font style emphasize in equations (see my comment above).
Consider aligning the entries of your matrices:\[\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1  \\ -1 &  1 \end{pmatrix}\quad\text{vs}\quad\begin{pmatrix} \phantom+1 & -1  \\ -1 & \phantom+1 \end{pmatrix}.\] This was achieved by introducing phantom plus signs in front of the positive 1-s. There are other ways to achieve this, e.g. using \begin{array}{r}, but arrays work differently than matrices, so it is a case-by-case decision.
There is a special \colon command to be used instead of :: \[f\colon A\to B\quad\text{vs}\quad f:A\to B.\] In introduced the command \: for that, so I can switch if necessary.
instead of giving very long definings, dare to go multi-line in placerd where it is not usual.
Consider controlling the spacing around big sum limits etc: \[y:=\sum_{i\in S(\mathcal P_0)} x_i\quad\text{vs}\quad y:=\sum_{\mathclap{i\in S(\mathcal P_0)}}x_i\] There is no need to have this big spacing left and right of the sum. So you can get rid of it using \mathclap.

title: Real representation theory
text:
We do real real representation theory.
Let \(G\) be a group and \(\phi:G\to\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}(V)\) a real representation. A matrix group \(G\subseteq\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}(V)\). Throughout we assume that \(\phi\) is irreducible, that, there is no subspace \(U\subset V\) with \(\phi(g)U\subseteq U\) for any \(g\in G\).
A map \(f:V\to V\) is equivariant if \(gf(v)=f(gv)\). They serve as isomorphisms between representations. That is, two matrx groups are considered as “the same” if there is an equivalerian map between them.
The centralizer \(C(G)\) is the set of maps \(f:V\to V\) that commute with all matrices in \(G\). Note that the centralizer is itself closed under additional and matrix multiplication and hence forms a ring. The famous Schur’s lemma states that the centralizer also enables permits inverses, which makes it a division algebra over the ground field. This is significant, because depending on the ground field, there are’t many division algebras. For example, over \(\Bbb C\), there is only \(\Bbb C\) itself, and so the centralizer over a complex-irreducible matrix group is (ismorphic) to \(\Bbb C\). In contrast, there are non-division rings over \(\Bbb R\), but those are well-understood. According tot he famous … theorem, a division algebra over \(\Bbb R\) is isomoprhic to either \(\Bbb R\), \(\Bbb C\) or \(\Bbb H\) (the quaternions).

This tells us that there is some more diversity in real representations than complex ones. In particular, we can sort real-irreducible representations into three bins: real, complex and quaternionic. Every group that has complex type can be promoted to one that has quaternionic type. For this, write it in complex form and replace each block by the corresponding quaterionic block.

Theorem.  An irreducbile matrix group \(G\) has \(C(G)\simeq \Bbb C\) (resp. \(C(G)\simeq \Bbb H\)) if and only if \(G\) has a basis-representation in which all elements are block matrices with blocks being \(2\times 2\)-matrix representations of \(\Bbb C\) (resp. \(4\times 4\)-matrix representations of \(\Bbb H\)). 

Suppose first that \(G\) has a representation with block-matrices. Then any diagonal block matrix whose block are of complex type commutes with \(G\).

title: Lecture – Geometry of Convex Polytopes
text:
When


Summer semester 2026  Every Wednesday, 10:30am – 12:00pm  All lecture dates here




Where\(\;\;\)


MPI Leipzig  Room G3 10



This course is conceived as a follow up on the block course “Convex Polytopes” by Bernd Sturmfels, though participation in the latter is not a prerequisite. You can find recordings of the block course behind the link.
See here for the lecture on the MPI website.

Description
Much of the appeal of polytope theory comes from the fact that a convex polytope is both a geometric and a combinatorial object. This lecture will focus on the geometric aspects of this interaction, to which there are two approaches:


the study of the metric properties of individual polytopes, such as edge lengths, dihedral angles, face shapes and volume, the relations between these quantities as well as the constraints imposed on them by the combinatorics.
the study of the geometric/topological properties of entire realization spaces, that is, the study of the ways in which a fixed combinatorial type can be realized or a given realizations can be deformed.

We shall follow both of these routes in four interconnected sections.
In the first part we take a look at the realization space of a convex polytope. We recall its descriptions as a semialgebraic set, discuss properties and the complexity one faces for high-dimensional polytopes. Eventually we prove the infamous universality theorem.
In the second part we consider polytopes specifically in dimension three. We first reprove Steinitz’ theorem on the combinatorial characterization of 3-polytopes, but in a way that reveals that the realization space (modulo isometries) is homeomorphic to \(\Bbb R^E\), where \(E\) is the number of edges of the polytope. The main tools employed are Tutte embeddings and the Maxwell-Cremona correspondence, of which we give a detailled account. All known constructions of this homeomorphism are highly non-canonical, which raises the question whether canonical parametrizations even exist. Partial solutions are known from Teichmüller theory, rigidity theory, the theory of circle packings, etc., and we will discuss some of them.
In the third part we approach realization spaces from the perspective of rigidity theory: what metric assumptions guarantee that the realization space (modulo isometries) has isolated points? We introduce the core concepts from rigidity theory, including the first-order analysis. We give an overview of the vaste landscape of rigidity results and conjectures, including theorems by Cauchy, Dehn, Gluck, Alexandrov, Whiteley, Connelly, Gortler, Minkowski and Stoker. We discuss the open problem of spherical Tutte embeddings and draw parallels to both canonical parameters and Wachspress Geometry.
In the last part we discuss the question of metric reconstruction of polytopes from partial combinatorial and metric data. We use tools from Wachspress Geometry (Wachspress coordinates, the Izemstiev matrix and the adjoint) to achieve partial reconstruction results.


Lectures and literature

Lecture 1 (April 17): introduction, realization spaces of polytopes, Lawrence extensions, non-prescribable facets, non-connected realization spaces, universality of realization spaces for polytopes and oriented matroids, von Staudt constructions

Bokowski, Ewald, Kleinschmidt; “On combinatorial and affine automorphisms of polytopes”. (first construction of a combinatorial type with non-realizable symmetries)
Richter-Gebert; “The Universality Theorems for Oriented Matroids and Polytopes”. (short monograph on universality results in oriented matroids and polytopes)
Richter-Gebert; “Realization Spaces of Polytopes”. (a much more elababorate monograph on realization spaces of polytopes)
Adiprasito, Padrol; “The universality theorem for neighborly polytopes”.

Lecture 2 (April 22): zonotopal universality, universality of 6-polytopes, projectively unique polytopes, compact realization spaces and applications to Kalai’s conjectures

Ziegler; “Non-rational configurations, polytopes, and surfaces”.
Adiprasito, Ziegler; “Many projectively unique polytopes”. (construction of infinitely many projectively unique polytopes in dimension 69)

Lecture 3 (May 6): realization spaces of 3-polytopes, Legrende-Steinitz theorem, circle-packing theorem, stresses, Maxwell-Cremona correspondence
Lecture 4 (May 11): Tutte embeddings, dimension computation for the realization space, canonical realizations, Rivin’s theorem for ideal hyperbolic polyhedra

Together with Georg Loho and Olivia Röhrig, we are organizing a 2-weeks hands-on workshop “Polyhedra in Lean” to take place August 24 – September 4, 2026 at FU Berlin.

We are supported by

Olivia Röhrig (leading PhD student, Zuse Institute Berlin)
John Maar (PhD student at TU Berlin)
Kilian Rueß (PhD student at UT Nürnberg)
